title: SINGH v PR KAHON LIMITED and Anor
text:
NOTE: This determination
contains an order prohibiting
publication of certain
information at paragraph [87]
IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY
WELLINGTON
I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI
TE WHANGANUI-A-TARA ROHE
[2026] NZERA 521
3311580
BETWEEN MANDEEP SINGH
Applicant
AND PR KAHON LIMITED
First Respondent
AND SATPAL SINGH
Second Respondent
Member of Authority: Claire English
Representatives: John Wood, advocate for the Applicant
Nikkii Flint, counsel for the Respondent
Investigation Meeting: 25 February and 16 March 2026 in Palmerston North
and by AVL
Submissions received: Up to 29 July 2026 from Applicant
Up to 28 July 2026 from Respondent
Determination: 04 August 2026
DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY
Employment Relationship Problem
[1] The applicant, Mr Mandeep Singh, was employed by the first respondent PR
Kahlon Limited (Kahlon) as a delivery driver based in Palmerton North. The second
respondent, Mr Satpal Singh, is one of two directors and one of two shareholders in
Kahlon and is an owner operator of the company. Mr Singh says that he was employed
by Kahlon from 21 July 2023 as a Class 1 van and truck driver. He says that he did not

begin to get paid until 20 August 2023. He then says he was paid a flat rate of 30 hours
per week regardless of the number of hours he actually worked, and he consistently
worked more than this.
[2] At the end of October 2023, Mr Singh was placed on a performance
improvement plan (PIP), focusing on matters such as filling out required paperwork
and providing proof of deliverers among other matters. At the end of May 2024, Kahlon
through Mr Satpal Singh, sought to meet with him again. Following a meeting, Mr
Singh was dismissed by letter on 18 June 2024, for a variety of performance concerns.
[3] Mr Singh raises claims against Kahlon and Mr Satpal Singh for unjustified
dismissal and unjustified disadvantage, as well as hurt, humiliation, and injury to
feelings, and lost wages in respect of this. He also raises claims for unpaid wages in
relation to work done, unpaid holiday pay, a penalty under the Wages Protection Act
1983 for failures to pay wages when due and for what are said to be unlawful deductions
from wages, a penalty for breaching his employment agreement, and a penalty for
breaches of good faith.
[4] He claims against Mr Satpal Singh that he was a person involved in a breach of
minimum standards, and seeks orders allowing him to recover from Mr Satpal Singh
personally any arrears of holiday pay.
[5] Kahlon and Mr Satpal Singh deny the claims. They say that Mr Singh was
employed on an hourly rate and paid in accordance with timesheets filled out by him
on a regular basis, which genuinely reflect the work that he performed. They also say
that Mr Singh was dismissed following a prolonged period of poor performance and
point to the PIP plan and email and text correspondence between him and Mr Satpal
Singh to show that he was not meeting performance standards over a prolonged period
of time.
The Authority’s investigation
[6] For the Authority’s investigation written witness statements were lodged from
Mr Singh, and his friend and co-worker Mr Ajaypal Singh. Mr Satpal Singh gave
evidence on behalf of himself and Kahlon. An interpreter was available to assist. All
witnesses answered questions under affirmation from me and the parties’
representatives. The representatives also gave closing submissions.

[7] As permitted by s 174E of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) this
determination has stated findings of fact and law, expressed conclusions on issues
necessary to dispose of the matter and specified orders made. It has not recorded all
evidence and submissions received.
The issues
[8] The issues requiring investigation and determination were:
(a) Was Mr Singh unjustifiably dismissed?
(b) Did Mr Singh suffer an unjustified disadvantage?
(c) If Kahlon’s actions were not justified (in respect of disadvantage and/or
dismissal), what remedies should be awarded, considering:
• Lost wages (subject to evidence of reasonable endeavours to mitigate
loss); and
• Compensation under s123(1)(c)(i) of the Act?
(d) If any remedies are awarded, should they be reduced (under s124 of the
Act) for blameworthy conduct by Mr Singh that contributed to the
situation giving rise to his grievance?
(e) Is there any final holiday pay owing to Mr Singh?
(f) Are any wage arrears owed to Mr Singh?
(g) Should penalties be awarded to Mr Singh because of any unlawful
deductions from wages, or breaches of the employment agreement?
(h) Should any penalties awarded be paid to Mr Singh personally?
(i) Was Mr Satpal Singh a person involved in a breach of minimum
standards?
(j) If so, should leave be granted to Mr Singh to recover from Mr Satpal
Singh personally any holiday pay found to be owing?
(k) Should either party contribute to the costs of representation of the other
party.
Background
Claim of Unpaid Training Period
[9] Mr Singh submits that he started working for Kahlon on 21 July 2023, but that
he was not paid for the work that he did. Mr Singh has provided a variety of
photographs, showing the inside of a truck cab, the view of the road from a truck cab,

and various wrapped parcels or goods for delivery, which he says shows that he was
working for Kahlon from 21 July onwards.
[10] Kahlon denies this. It says that Mr Singh arrived in New Plymouth on about 20
July 2023, but that he was not able to start work then because he did not have a New
Zealand driver’s licence, and nor had he completed the required staff checks used by
Mainfreight, the provider that Kahlon worked for. Mr Mandeep Singh received a New
Zealand driver’s licence and successfully completed the required staff checks on 4
September 2023. Kahlon states that he started working for it on 4 September, as this
was the first date he was able to drive vehicles on behalf of Mainfreight.
[11] Mr Satpal Singh says that Mr Singh did a short “meet and great” with him on
21 July, and filled in certain induction forms, but this was the extent of the engagement
and did not amount to work.
[12] Mr Mandeep Singh says that he arranged with another driver to sit with them in
their truck cab while they drove and performed loading and deliveries. Mr Mandeep
Singh says that he and the other driver, who did not attend the investigation meeting or
provide evidence, would work together for up to 11 hours every day, this amounted to
him performing work for Kahlon, and he should be paid for all this time in full.
[13] Mr Mandeep Singh accepted in oral evidence that this was not requested by Mr
Satpal Singh, or even arranged by him, but was an arrangement he had reached with
that other driver. Mr Satpal Singh says that he was not aware of this, he neither knew
nor authorised Mr Mandeep Singh to accompany this other driver, and that there was
no business need for this. Mr Satpal Singh also stated that 11 hours per day was longer
than that other driver would normally work and it made no sense that, if Mr Mandeep
Singh was in fact assisting with deliveries, that that driver would take longer than if he
had been working alone.
[14] I am not persuaded that any such actions by Mr Mandeep Singh amounted to
work performed on behalf of Kahlon such that Mr Mandeep Singh is entitled to be paid
wages for this period. Mr Mandeep Singh states that he arranged with another driver
to sit in that driver’s truck cab while that other driver drove and/or performed deliveries.
He accepts that this was not an arrangement between him and Kahlon. There is no
evidence that this was necessary for Kahlon’s business or benefited it in any way.

Fundamentally, Mr Mandeep Singh’s own evidence is that he was never required by
Mr Satpal Singh to do this, and he never told Mr Satpal Singh or was authorised by Mr
Satpal Singh in doing this. Rather, Mr Mandeep Singh states that this was an
arrangement he entered into with the other driver without involving Mr Satpal Singh.
For these reasons, I decline to find that he was performing work for Khalon during this
time, or that any obligation to pay him arose from his actions.
[15] I also note that the pay records and work chat records record that Mr Mandeep
Singh started work and was paid from 4 September 2023, as Kahlon maintains,
following the granting of Mr Mandeep Singh’s New Zealand drivers’ licence and
successful completion of Mainfreight staff checks. These documents tend to support
Kahlon’s position that Mr Mandeep Singh did not start working for it until 4 September
2023, as this was the earliest date that Mr Mandeep Singh was paid for, and he was not
part of the work chat records prior to this. I will return to the issue of logbooks and
timesheets at a later point.
Claim of Systemic Underpayment for Work Done
[16] Mr Mandeep Singh states that throughout his employment, he was paid at a flat
rate of 30 hours per week, regardless of the hours he actually worked each week. Mr
Mandeep Singh says that his vehicle logbooks and handwritten time-sheets show that
he worked significantly longer than this, and he should be paid for the extra hours he
actually worked.
[17] A letter of offer and an individual employment agreement were in evidence.
Both documents provided that Mr Mandeep Singh would be paid an hourly rate, and
his normal hours of work would be from 8.00 am to 3.30 pm, Monday to Friday
(equating to 37.5 hours per week), with the possibility for some hours of work in excess
of this depending on business needs. Despite Mr Mandeep Singh stating that his
employment agreement provided for a standard payment of 30 hours per week, I find
this was not the case. I also note that the agreement did not provide for any guaranteed
minimum hours of work.
[18] Kahlon denied that Mr Mandeep Singh worked more hours than he was paid
for. Mr Satpal Singh was clear in his understanding that Mr Mandeep Singh was paid
on an hourly basis, and his pay varied from week to week to reflect his hours. Mr Satpal

Singh pointed to Mr Mandeep Singh’s payslips and associated hours recorded in
timesheets and the payroll system. These showed that Mr Mandeep Singh’s hours of
work each week varied from a low of 35.5 hours to a high of 47 hours pay. There were
no weeks when Mr Mandeep Singh was paid 30 hours per week, and his lowest paid
week was when he was paid for 35.5 hours of work. Of the 39 weekly payslips that
were in evidence over the duration of Mr Mandeep Singh’s employment, for 29 of these
weeks, he was paid for more than 40 hours of work per week. Even when the payslips
were put to Mr Mandeep Singh, he maintained that Kahlon paid him a flat rate of 30
hours per week, and he could not explain why he took that position in the face of
contrary evidence.
[19] Mr Mandeep Singh relied on hours he had recorded in vehicle log books to
support his claim that he had worked more hours than were recorded in his timesheets
and the payroll system.
[20] Mr Mandeep Singh stated in his evidence that the logbooks recorded the hours
he had actually worked, and should be relied on as evidence of hours actually worked
wherever his vehicle log book entries showed that he had worked more hours than his
timesheets showed.
[21] There was mixed and conflicting evidence at the investigation meeting about
the vehicle logbooks. Mr Mandeep Singh was required to keep a vehicle logbook to
record his driving hours. He was also required to fill out timesheets, which timesheets
were the basis of his weekly pay.
[22] The timesheets are aligned with the weekly pay received. The logbooks
sometimes differ from the timesheets, although having compared logbooks and
timesheet entries, I am not persuaded that the difference is as great, or as consistent as
is submitted by Mr Mandeep Singh.
[23] Mr Mandeep Singh said that Mr Satpal Singh had repeatedly instructed him on
how to fill out his logbooks, and he was instructed to fill out his logbooks in a way that
was false. He was highly critical of Mr Satpal Singh and said that Mr Satpal Singh had
instructed him to not start the logbook entry for each day until he started driving, which
was usually around 7.30 am, to record break times and non-driving times, and to end
the logbook entries for the day when he stopped driving. Mr Mandeep Singh said that
this meant the logbooks were false and inaccurate because he would arrive at the depot

before he started driving at 7.30 am, considered he was still working if he took breaks
while driving (there was usually a break between morning and afternoon) and did not
immediately leave the depot once he stopped driving in the afternoon but might have
other tasks to do. He says that the instruction not to record non-driving hours in the
logbook amounts to falsification of the logbook.
[24] It was clear from Mr Mandeep Singh’s evidence and confirmed through
questioning, that he had been repeatedly instructed by Mr Satpal Singh not to record
non-driving hours in vehicle logbooks. This does not amount to inaccurate completion
of the logbooks, nor does it amount to falsifying the logbooks. It simply reflects that
vehicle logbooks are a tool for recording driving hours, not working hours more
generally.
[25] Mr Mandeep Singh was repeatedly unable to explain or differentiate between
the vehicle logbooks and the more general timesheets in his evidence.
[26] Mr Satpal Singh agreed that he had spoken with Mr Mandeep Singh on several
occasions about how to fill out the vehicle logbooks, and how it was important that he
did not record time in the logbooks that was not driving time. Mr Satpal Singh said that
the timesheets however, were a record of all hours worked whether driving or not.
[27] Mr Satpal Singh said that he also spoke with Mr Mandeep Singh on several
occasions about filling out his weekly timesheets, as he was aware of times when Mr
Mandeep Singh had failed to record work done in his timesheets, particularly that he
was entitled to claim one hour’s pay each week for time spent washing his truck and
for training, and when he was aware that Mr Satpal Singh had not claimed for these
instances in his timesheet, he would adjust (that is, increase) his weekly pay
accordingly. This was supported by notes made in the relevant payroll reports. Mr
Satpal Singh also stated that there were times when Mr Mandeep Singh had overstated
the work that he had done in his timesheets, in particular instances when he had driven
the work van or truck to do personal shopping and deliveries around the middle of the
day. Again, there were supporting notes in the payroll reports about this.
[28] I do not understand Mr Mandeep Singh to dispute this.
[29] Mr Mandeep Singh maintained, under repeated questioning, that the logbooks
he had filled out were false. Yet he also maintained that they contained an accurate

record of his hours of work where they were in his favour and I should rely on them to
order the payment of additional wages to him. When I put it to him directly that there
was a contradiction in his evidence on this point, he was unable to explain his position
further.
[30] I also received evidence from Mr Ajaypal Singh as to Mr Mandeep Singh’s
actual hours of work. Mr Ajaypal Singh gave evidence that Mr Mandeep Singh used
to start work at 4.00 or 4.30 am and finish work at 8.00 pm or 9.00 pm at night, 6 days
per week. When asked how he knew this, he said that he had not seen Mr Mandeep
Singh working these hours, but this was what Mr Mandeep Singh had told him. He said
that sometimes, he would pick Mr Mandeep Singh up from the depot after 7.00 pm at
night and drive him home, as Mr Mandeep Singh did not have a car, however, he did
not see him working. This is not first-hand evidence, and is fundamentally inconsistent
with Mr Mandeep Singh’s claims before the Authority as to his own hours of work.
Insofar as any weight can be placed on this, it tends to suggest that Mr Mandeep Singh
has exaggerated his hours of work.
[31] When I consider the evidence of both parties overall, I am not persuaded that
there is reliable evidence to support Mr Mandeep Singh’s claims that he worked hours
beyond those he was paid for. The fundamental basis of Mr Mandeep Singh’s evidence
was that he was paid a standard amount of 30 hours per week, because that was the
minimum required by his employment agreement, and in fact, his hours worked were
in excess of this. The evidence established that the entire basis for this claim is simply
incorrect and is not what occurred. Mr Mandeep Singh was paid significantly in excess
of 30 hours per week for all weeks worked, on an hourly basis with a moderate amount
of variation showing from week to week. Pay was based on timesheets filled out by
Mr Mandeep Singh himself. Kahlon has actively and consistently used its payroll
system to make notes about the hours worked and the pay made to Mr Mandeep Singh,
including adjustments both up and down to account for additional work done where this
was known but not recorded and where personal time was taken during the workday.
This is not improper and does not suggest systemic underpayment.
[32] I also do not consider that I can safely rely on Mr Mandeep Singh’s account of
his own hours of work in circumstances where he himself states that contemporaneous
records have been falsified by him except where they are in his favour. On balance, I

consider that Mr Mandeep Singh’s claims that he has worked in excess of the hours he
was paid for are not made out.
Claims of unlawful deduction from final pay and failure to pay holiday pay
[33] Mr Mandeep Singh’s final payslip shows that he was paid a lump sum in holiday
pay, and that the sum of $283.59 was deducted from his final pay. Mr Mandeep Singh
stated that deductions from his wages were for an unknown purpose and should not
have been made at all. He seeks reimbursement and penalties.
[34] The evidence at hearing was that deductions were made from Mr Mandeep
Singh’s pay, both of which related to fees for a Class 5 driver’s licence course. Kahlon
agreed to pay the cost of this training up-front, to be repaid by Mr Mandeep Singh at a
later date. The training was not required by Kahlon, who did not need or require Mr
Mandeep Singh to have a Class 5 licence. When this was put to him, Mr Mandeep
Singh accepted that this was what the deductions were for, and that he had agreed to
proceed with the training on this basis.
[35] That being the case, I find that the claim of unlawful deduction from wages is
not made out. No orders are made.
[36] Mr Mandeep Singh has also made a claim for payment of his final holiday pay,
stating in his statement of problem that he sought as a remedy “final holiday pay –
TBC”. Kahlon has provided a copy of Mr Mandeep Singh’s final payslip showing that
his final holiday pay was paid to him. This was not pursued further in evidence or
initial submissions. When I asked Mr Mandeep Singh to quantify his claims for wages,
submissions referred to a calculation of 8% holiday pay on all underpayments of wages,
less the amount of holiday pay received in his final pay. As I have not found any
underpayments of wages, I likewise find that the claim for holiday pay calculated on
them is not made out. No orders are made.
Was Mr Mandeep Singh unjustifiably dismissed?
[37] I now come to consider the ending of Mr Mandeep Singh’s employment.
Throughout his employment, beginning at the end of October 2023, Kahlon raised
performance concerns with Mr Mandeep Singh. Concerns included incomplete

deliveries, failing to scan freight when delivering, failing to obtain valid signatures,
entering incorrect details, failure to update status information, and producing proof-of-
delivery that did not match actual delivery times or locations, and failing to return
pallets when required.
[38] Mr Satpal Singh says these issues generated complaints from customers and
Mainfreight. Mr Satpal Singh said he provided additional assistance to Mr Mandeep
Singh to help him understand the requirements of the role, including giving him
repeated hands-on training on how to use the scanning devices, repeating directions
multiple times, providing directions in written form and in the group chat, asking him
to repeat directions back to ensure they were understood, and providing extra time.
Copies of the work chat are in evidence showing that Mr Satpal Singh raised these
issues, and received various responses from both Mr Mandeep Singh and others, in both
English and Punjabi.
[39] Mr Satpal Singh also raised concerns over Mr Mandeep Singh’s driving,
including concerns that he did not follow site speed limits causing customer complaints,
failure to safely use a forklift despite training resulting in Mr Satpal Singh loading Mr
Manpreet Singh’s truck for him in the mornings, failure to complete, submit, and in
some cases keep vehicle logbooks despite this being repeatedly discussed with him,
repeated freight damage, and accidents resulting in damage to customer roofs, spouting,
and concrete. Mr Manpreet Singh accepts that he caused some of these incidents by
way of hitting structures with his vehicle, but not others. He did accept that he was
banned from two customer sites as a result.
[40] On 25 October 2023, Mr Satpal Singh sent Mr Mandeep Singh an email inviting
him to a meeting to discuss various performance issues, including discussing a PIP or
performance improvement plan. They met to discuss this on 29 October. A document
described as a written warning entitled “Employee Performance Review” was issued
on 5 November 2023. This was signed by both parties. Mr Mandeep Singh says he did
not understand this, as it was in English. This is disputed by Mr Satpal Singh who says
that he and Mr Mandeep Singh were able to speak to each other directly in Punjabi as
needed.
[41] Documents, particularly emails and work chat messages, show that Mr Satpal
Singh continued to raise these types of issues over the next four or five months, and

particularly to raise issues with Mr Mandeep Singh about his completion of point-of-
delivery information, which it was said remained either missing or incorrect when
completed. Mr Mandeep Singh had no particular comment on this concern, although
in his in-person evidence, he said that messages in the work chat were simply general
advice and had no particular relevance to him. The work chat messages do show him
engaging using a mix of English and Pubjabi.
[42] On 7 May 2024, Mr Satpal Singh emailed Mr Mandeep Singh and issued him
with a final written warning over his failures to correctly provide point-of-delivery
information. The email referred to “prior serious verbal and written discussions” and
stated “If you are unsure about this talk to me in the office or in person….It’s the process
you are missing which you need to follow. I seek your urgent attention to resolve this
matter.”
[43] On 25 May 2024, Mr Satpal Singh emailed Mr Mandeep Singh to set up a
meeting to discuss the continuing performance issues, including ongoing concerns
about point-of-delivery information.
[44] On 26 May 2024, Mr Mandeep Singh emailed Mr Satpal Singh with an ACC
injury claim form, recording that he had slipped going down the stairs at home and hurt
his knee. The form stated he was unfit for work for 14 days. Mr Satpal Singh
responded, thanking him for sending through the form, advising that 80% of his wages
would be paid for the first week, and advising that the planned meeting would be
postponed and he would be in touch about this via email.
[45] Mr Mandeep Singh also completed and provided to Mr Satpal Singh an
inspection checklist showing he had completed a weekly inspection of his vehicle. Mr
Satpal Singh reprimanded Mr Mandeep Singh for this, pointing out that as he was off
work, he had not in fact preformed this inspection and the vehicle had been inspected
by Mr Satpal Singh himself, meaning that the form was essentially a false record. There
was no explanation given as to why Mr Mandeep Singh did this.
[46] On 8 June 2024, Mr Mandeep Singh’s advocate contacted Mr Satpal Singh,
asking for further information. A letter was provided on 10 June 2024, setting out an
agenda for what was described as a formal meeting and “follow up on existing PIP
plan”, which was a list of the performance concerns set out above. A meeting was held
with Mr Mandeep Singh and his advocate on 10 June 2024. During that meeting, Mr

Mandeep Singh said that he did not remember being on a PIP. The training that had
been provided was discussed, and Mr Satpal Singh proposed another warning and
further PIP, but indicated this would need to be for a short period of time given the
seriousness of the issues.
[47] Mr Mandeep Singh then raised concerns that he had not been properly paid for
all the hours he had worked. Mr Satpal Singh described this claim as a “diversion” and
a “serious conflict of interest”.
[48] The following day on 11 June 2024, Mr Mandeep’s advocate asked that Mr
Mandeep Singh be rostered to work, as he was fully fit.
[49] On 12 June 2024, Mr Satpal Singh replied. He said that Mr Mandeep Singh’s
return to work had not been agreed, “until Employer see the positive approach from the
employee to fix those issues”. Instead of moving on to discuss an improvement plan,
there was “then big conflict raised in formal meeting and employee announced the fake
allegations to the Employer in formal meeting. So, he can’t get back to work.”
[50] The advocate then asked if Mr Mandeep Singh would be paid while he was
suspended from work.
[51] There was no further correspondence between the parties. Mr Satpal Singh said
that he was waiting for Mr Mandeep Singh and his advocate to provide any final
comments, and a plan for improvement in relation to the performance issues raised. Mr
Mandeep Singh says that he was never asked to provide any feedback or a plan. Mr
Satpal Singh says that he thought he had been clear in the meeting on 10 June that he
would consider any feedback or proposed plan, and this was also mentioned in his
follow-up email later that same day when he provided copies of relevant documents
including the previous PIP plan, as well as email correspondence discussing
performance matters with Mr Mandeep Singh.
[52] On 18 June 2024, Mr Satpal Singh sent a final letter to Mr Mandeep Singh via
his advocate, terminating his employment with immediate effect. The letter stated:
In our formal meeting on 10th June 2024 along with your representative Sunny
Seghal, you didn’t comment at all on the above identified serious issues raised
by your employer and have no plan mentioned to fix these issues to be able to
continue the employment with PR Kahlon ltd. Therefore we confirm as a
responsible employer, having you on board we can’t compromise the Road

safety of others considering the nature of your driving Job and business
interests of our clients.
[53] Due to the immediate nature of the dismissal, Mr Mandeep Singh raises a claim
for payment of four week’s contractual notice in addition to the other remedies he seeks.
[54] When considering Mr Mandeep’s claim that he was unjustifiably dismissed, the
test is whether the employer’s actions were what a fair and reasonable employer could
have done in all the circumstances at the time. I must consider whether:
a. Kahlon sufficiently investigated the allegations against Mr Mandeep
Singh;
b. Kahlon raised the concerns it had with him before dismissing him;
c. Kahlon gave Mr Mandeep Singh a reasonable opportunity to respond to
its concerns before dismissal; and
d. Genuinely considered Mr Mandeep Singh’s explanations, if any, before
dismissing.
[55] I may also consider any other factors I think appropriate. I must not determine
a dismissal to be unjustified solely because of defects in the process followed if the
defects did not result in Mr Mandeep Singh being treated unfairly.
[56] I find that Kahlon did sufficiently investigate the allegations against Mr
Mandeep Singh, and there was consistent contemporaneous documentary evidence of
a variety of performance concerns. These concerns were clear, related directly to the
duties Mr Mandeep Singh was required to perform as a delivery driver, and in most if
not all cases, the required or remedial action was also clear from the very nature of the
concerns themselves. The concerns also persisted over time. I find that there was
sufficient evidence to justify performance concerns being raised.
[57] Kahlon did raise its concerns with Mr Mandeep Singh prior to dismissing him.
They were set out in a letter inviting him to a formal meeting, at the meeting itself, and
a follow-up email sent to his advocate with significant supporting documentation.
[58] I have more concerns about whether Kahlon truly gave Mr Manpreet Singh a
reasonable opportunity to respond, and whether it genuinely considered his
explanations before dismissing him. Mr Mandeep Singh did not respond to the

performance concerns raised with him. He took the position that he did not know about
them, did not understand the impact of the PIP and written warnings Mr Satpal Singh
had issued him with and how these might impact his employment, and overall that he
did not understand these matters because of his difficulties understanding English, both
written and spoken.
[59] Mr Satpal Singh rejected that Mr Mandeep Singh’s lack of understanding was
genuine. He said that he and Mr Mandeep Singh were able to communicate in Punjabi
where this was needed and that Mr Mandeep Singh participated in the work chats in
both English and Punjabi, showing that he did understand the discussions going on
there. Mr Mandeep Singh maintained that he did not fully understand all the documents
written in English, and noted that the work chat was in a mix of Punjabi and English.
[60] Having considered all this, I note that Mr Satpal Singh in his written evidence
was highly critical of what he described as Mr Manpreet Singh’s “limited English
ability”, said a major concern he had about Mr Mandeep Singh’s on-going employment
was “his difficulty communicating in English, both verbally and in writing”, and that
“Mandeep’s communication skills remained a significant barrier to safe and efficient
performance”. The lack of English proficiency was described by Mr Satpal Singh as
being serious enough that it was a performance concern.
[61] Having been so highly aware of Mr Mandeep Singh’s difficulties with
communicating in English, Mr Satpal Singh nevertheless chose to communicate
performance and disciplinary concerns with him in English, rather than the Punjabi in
which they were both fluent. While I do not accept that Mr Manpreet Singh was
completely unaware of the performance concerns raised with him as he suggested, I
also consider it likely that he did not understand how seriously Kahlon and Mr Satpal
Singh took these concerns, and nor did he truly understand that on-going performance
concerns could eventually lead to the ending of his employment.
[62] Similarly, I have concerns about how the meeting on 10 June 2024 was left. Mr
Satpal Singh was hoping and expecting to receive a substantive response to the
performance concerns, and some type of plan for improvement going forward. He
believed he had communicated to Mr Mandeep Singh and his advocate that he was open
to discussing this and would give them time to provide such information. Mr Mandeep

Singh and his advocate say they did not understand that Mr Satpal Singh was waiting
on this information or response from them.
[63] Having reviewed the correspondence, I have formed the view that this
opportunity for further engagement was not clearly expressed by Mr Satpal Singh.
[64] For both these reasons, I find that when considered overall, Kahlon did not
provide Mr Mandeep Singh with a reasonable opportunity to respond before dismissing
him, nor did it genuinely consider his explanations before dismissing him.
Accordingly, I find on balance that Mr Mandeep Singh’s dismissal was unjustified.
[65] However, I do not discount the evidence of his performance concerns, and will
return to this when considering contribution.
Was Mr Mandeep Singh unjustifiably disadvantaged by being suspended?
[66] Mr Mandeep Singh raises a claim that he was unjustifiably disadvantaged by
being suspended without pay by Kahlon. He says this was unilateral, and in breach of
the terms of his employment agreement, which provided that suspension needed to be
both on pay, and where “necessary for the protection of its operational and business
interests”.1 He refers to the period at the end of his employment.
[67] Kahlon says that from 26 May 2024 to 10 June 2024, Mr Mandeep Singh was
on ACC-related sick leave and no additional payment is owing to him for this period.
The relevant payslip from immediately prior to this period shows that Mr Mandeep
Singh was paid for two days of sick leave, dated as being 20 May 2024 and 24 May
2024, as well as ordinary pay for the remainder of that time. Kahlon states that he was
receiving ACC payments for the remainder of that time. On the basis of the documents
before me, I find that the claim for unpaid sick leave and/or unpaid suspension for this
time period is not made out.
[68] Kahlon says that from 11 June to 18 June 2024, Mr Mandeep Singh was placed
on paid special leave. Kahlon says that this paid special leave occurred only after him
and his advocate had been given an opportunity to comment, was paid, and was
necessary for the protection of Kahlon’s business interests in all the circumstances,
1 At clause 21 of the employment agreement.

particularly its view that he was not driving safely. Accordingly, if this did amount to
suspension, it was justifiable and done in accordance with the employment agreement.
[69] Mr Mandeep Singh says that he was suspended without consultation on 12 June
2024, when Mr Satpal Singh advised by email that because of the unresolved matters
between the parties “he can’t get back to work”. Mr Mandeep Singh says that the lack
of consultation amounts to an unjustified disadvantage.
[70] On balance, I find that this claim is made out. The correspondence between the
parties occurred via email, where Mr Satpal Singh directs Mr Mandeep Singh to remain
away from the workplace. There is no opportunity for consultation, or any request for
feedback or suggestion that this state of affairs could be reconsidered, that I can see in
the correspondence. This was also in circumstances where Mr Mandeep Singh’s
advocate had advised that he was now fit to return to work. Accordingly, I find that
this second period of suspension was unjustified due to the lack of consultation.
[71] I requested that the relevant payslip for the period 11 June to 18 June 2024 was
provided. I was advised that there was only the final payslip, and that the system was
unable to provide a breakdown, but that the final payslip include payment for the final
week of work from 11 to 18 June 2024, and accrued entitlements. The payslip in
question referred to a single payment made on 16 July 2024 of $3,638.30 gross which
appeared to be final holiday pay. Submissions on behalf of the applicant also referred
to this sum as being for final holiday pay. The payslip also referred to the payment of
0.00 hours of ordinary pay.
[72] The applicant’s position is that he was never paid for his final week of work
when he was suspended. On balance, the payslip provided by Khalon supports that
submission. The relevant clause in Mr Manpreet Singh’s employment agreement
provides that suspension is to be “on full pay”, and suspension without pay can only be
considered in certain circumstances and after at least two weeks have passed, which
was not the case here. Accordingly, my view is that Mr Manpreet Singh’s claim for
payment of wages from 11 June to 18 June is made out.
[73] Mr Manpreet Singh submits that, based on his employment agreement which
referred to “permanent hours…from 08.00 am to 03.30 pm”, paid at the rate of $29.66
per hour, his minimum contractual weekly wage equates to $1,038.10 gross, and that
for the 6 days between 11 to 18 June 2024, this amounts to $1,245.72 gross. This is a

reasonable claim in all the circumstances, and in the absence of any other records from
the respondent, orders for payment are made accordingly.
Remedies
[74] Having found that Mr Mandeep Singh has established a personal grievance for
unjustified dismissal, I must now consider the issue of remedies. In the statement of
problem, he sought the payment of 4 weeks wages in an unspecified sum, plus lost
wages in an unspecified sum, plus holiday pay on these awards. No further detail of
the amounts sought was provided in submissions. My view is that this is a claim for
reimbursement under s 128 of the Act, which provides that where an employee has a
personal grievance, and has lost remuneration because of it, the Authority must order
the employer to pay to the employee the lessor of a sum equal to that lost remuneration
or to three months’ ordinary time remuneration.
[75] Given the limited evidence on this matter, on balance, I consider that it is
appropriate to award Mr Mandeep Singh the equivalent of 3 months’ ordinary time
remuneration. It is submitted for Mr Mandeep Singh that this amounts to 13 weeks pay
at the contractual rate of 35 hours per week and $29.66 per hour. This amounts to a
sum of $13,495.30 gross. Given that this is consistent with the provisions of the
employment agreement, and Mr Mandeep Singh’s wages in fact varied from week to
week, my view is that this is a reasonable claim. Orders are made accordingly.
[76] For completeness, I note that Mr Mandeep Singh also sought the payment of
four weeks notice, later reduced to two weeks, and holiday pay calculated on the three
month’s compensatory sum. Insofar as these amounts claim for more than the
equivalent of three months’ ordinary time remuneration, I decline to award them. No
further orders are made.
[77] I must also consider the claim for compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity,
and injury to feelings in accordance with s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act. Mr Mandeep Singh
gave evidence as to the impact of his termination on him. He said that he enjoyed
working, and that he did not know what to do once he had lost his job. He described
having to rely on his partner for financial assistance and receiving food from his local
temple. He said that he stopped seeing friends and socialising and found this a difficult
experience. I accept his evidence. I consider that a moderate award would be $17,000
in all the circumstances. I consider that I should award a further amount of $1,000 in

compensation for the unjustified suspension, taking into account that the suspension
then “ran on” into the facts leading to the unjustified dismissal for which I have also
made an award, and that, insofar as I have found the relevant claims to have been made
out, awards have separately been made for unpaid wages. This leads to a total
compensatory award of $18,000 before taking account of contribution.
[78] Having made these awards, I now need to consider contribution in accordance
with s 124 of the Act, which provides that remedies may be reduced if I find that the
actions of the employee contributed to the situation that gave rise to the personal
grievance claim.
[79] I find that Mr Mandeep Singh’s actions did contribute to the situation that gave
rise to his dismissal. Kahlon provided a consistent documentation trail showing that
performance concerns had been raised with Mr Mandeep Singh throughout his
employment. These issues were not seriously disputed by Mr Mandeep Singh, even at
hearing. I note that there was photographic evidence showing damage to vehicles,
including scrapes and dents. Some of this was admitted by Mr Mandeep Singh, who
also admitted at least one instance where he collided with a customer’s building, and
was banned from another customer’s site because of unsafe driving. Safe and accurate
driving is not a matter where Mr Mandeep Singh’s lack of proficiency with the English
language comes into play, especially in circumstances where he himself held multiple
classes of licence, and had sought out further driver training to secure a further class of
licence. Likewise I consider that the repeated requests by Mr Satpal Singh over many
months that Mr Manpreet Sigh scan parcels on delivery using a hand-held scanner may
reasonably be regarded as being made out on the facts, and could and should have been
able to be performed by Mr Manpreet Singh as a key part of his role.
[80] I am cognisant of the repeated efforts that Kahlon and Mr Satpal Singh went to
in providing training in the requirements of the job, and in stating the expectations of
the employer repeatedly over several months, with no apparent improvement even in
matters of safe and accident-free driving, which was the fundamental requirement of
the job. Accordingly, I find that a reduction of 25% is appropriate to account for Mr
Mandeep Singh’s contribution the situation that he found himself in. Remedies
awarded to him will be reduced accordingly.

Other matters
[81] In the statement of problem, penalties were sought for breaches of the Wages
Protection Act 1983 by failing to pay wages when due and/or for making unlawful
deductions from wages. I have found that these claims were not made out. Penalties
were also sought for an unspecified breach of the employment agreement. Insofar as
this may be in reference to the alleged failure to pay wages, I have found this was not
paid out, and if in relation to the matter of suspension, I have awarded remedies
separately for this matter.
[82] Penalties were also sought for a breach of good faith. The breaches of good
faith were said to be the charging of a premium for the job, which the claim was later
withdrawn, failing to pay Mr Mandeep Singh for a training period, which I have found
was not made out, unjustified dismissal and unjustified suspension, both of which I
have dealt with separately and awarded remedies separately. The threshold for the
award of a penalty in relation to a breach of good faith is high, and there is no indication
that the matters which were made out would have reached this threshold, being as they
were singular and unrepeated. I have also received no submissions as to why penalties
should be awarded for matters where other more directly available remedies have
already been given. On balance, I find that penalties are either not available, or to the
extent that they might be available, it would be inappropriate to make further awards.
No further orders are made.
[83] The statement of problem also sought declarations that Mr Satpal Singh and/or
Kahlon had breached minimum employment standards, a declaration that Mr Satpal
Singh was a person involved in a breach as defined in s 142Y of the Act, and that leave
be granted to recover certain monies from Mr Satpal Singh personally under s 142W of
the Act. As I have not found any breaches of minimum standards were made out, I
make no further findings on these matters.
[84] Interest on wage arrears was sought. As I have declined to uphold the claims
for unpaid wages, it follows that I also decline to award interest. No orders are made.
[85] Mr Manpreet Singh seeks the reimbursement of his filing fee of $71.55. As he
has achieved success in this matter, he is entitled to the reimbursement of this sum.
Orders are made accordingly.

Non-Publication Orders
[86] During the course of the proceedings, the respondents filed various information
with the Authority about the running of the business and its financial affairs. They
sought non-publication orders be made in respect of this information, which I
understand is not opposed.
[87] The information filed by the respondents about the business of Kahlon is
commercial-in-confidence information. I direct that it is not to be published, and nor is
it to be published, used, or shared by the applicant in any other forum or matter.
Orders
[88] Mr Mandeep Singh has a personal grievance in that he was unjustifiably
dismissed, and unjustifiably suspended.
[89] PR Kahlon Limited is ordered to pay to Mr Mandeep Singh within 28 days of
the date of this determination :
a. The sum of $934.29 gross for wages lost as a result of unpaid suspension
taking into account the reduction for contribution;
b. The sum of $10,121.48 gross as compensation for lost remuneration
taking into account the reduction for contribution;
c. The sum of $13,500 as compensation for hurt and humiliation taking
into account the reduction for contribution;
d. The sum of $71.55 as reimbursement of the filing fee.
Costs
[90] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs
between themselves. I note that for the purposes of costs, the investigation meeting
took place over one and a half days.
[91] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on
costs is needed, the applicant may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on
costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that
memorandum the respondent will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum.
On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate
costs between themselves may be granted.

[92] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so,
on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment
upwards or downwards.2
